text.p: The following are the main stories from Monday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Finance Minister Theo Waigel says Germany will meet the Maastricht criteria estimating this year's public deficit at 2.9 percent of GDP
- The Federation of German Industry called on the government to push through reforms in the energy sector and to stick to its plans for deregulation to make it more competitive
- Pensions in Germany could become increasingly more expensive to support. The Frankfurt Institute warns pension reformers in the CDU not to make a mistake
HANDELSBLATT
- Row over "holes" in the budget. The SPD has called on Finance Minister Theo Waigel to end what they called "financial chaos" and create a supplementary budget
- The SPD finance coordinator and Hamburg mayor Henning Voscherau called on his party leader Oskar Lafontaine to reach a compromise over tax reforms with the ruling coalition
- Labour Minister Norbert Bluem seeks a consensus on his proposed pension reform plans with his party the CDU's coalition partners the CSU and FDP and opposition SPD
- Number of visitors to Cebit trade fair has risen this year
- Every third employee working for Apple computers will be made redundant
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG

- The CSU, Christian Social Union in Bavaria, will have to beward of the Free Voters. The party that includes some former CSU members already established in local councils has said its candidates plan to stand in elections for the Bavarian state assembly
- Bavarian Finance Minister Erwin Huber called for an agreement between the federal government and regional states, committing each state to an obligation to fulfil the Maastricht criteria

- Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber said he did not want to stand for the chancellorship in the next general election. The CSU politician rejected speculation he was be a potential candidate as "ridiculous"
- Shareholder value is no longer a distant term for Germany's biggest firms. Study on DAX firms shows the top earners to be Veba and Hoechst
- German parliament will debate first part of proposed reforms of pensions and tax systems this week
DIE WELT
- Chances of a tax agreement increase. The government and opposition SPD have shown willingness for a swift agreement
- Pinning their hopes on disillusionment with one party. Free Voters party wants to break the CSU's absolute majority on regional-level Bavaria

- Shortly before Bonn's ability to meet the Maastricht criteria for EMU is discussed in Brussels, there are renewed signs Germany will not make the grade. According to an internal document from the Chancellery Germany's budget deficit will be over 4.15 percent of GDP in 1997 -- overstepping the prescribed maximum of three percent of GDP
- Germany pays by far highest EU contributions
- DGB German trade union federation rejects CDU's plans to reform pension systems including proposal to drop level to 64 percent
